opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me back.

I think the single most important thing is to stop collapsing the forecast into one number. When someone says "AGI by 2032," listeners hear a prediction, a date to hold you to, when what you actually have in mind is a whole probability distribution, and usually a very wide one. So I'd encourage forecasters to give at least a few points on it: when you think there's a 10% chance it's happened by, when 50%, when 90%. That immediately conveys two things a single date hides: how early it could plausibly come, and how long the tail is.

That tail matters a lot. AGI timeline distributions tend to be right-skewed: there's a lot of probability mass in the next decade or two, but then a long stretch where it might take much longer, because some key ingredient turns out to be harder than expected. If you only report a median, people miss both the uncomfortable near-term probability and the real possibility that it's quite far off. And for decision-making, those ends of the distribution are often what matter most. If there's a 10 or 20% chance of something transformative within a few years, that's enough to justify serious preparation now, even if your median is later.

Second, I'd like to see people be clearer about *what* they're forecasting. "AGI" means very different things to different people: a system that can do most remote knowledge work, one that can automate AI research itself, or something broadly superhuman. A lot of apparent disagreement between forecasters is really disagreement about definitions. If you specify the capability, ideally in terms of something observable, your numbers become comparable with other people's, and checkable later.

Third, explain where the uncertainty comes from. Is it uncertainty about whether scaling continues, about compute and investment, about whether new algorithmic ideas are needed, about regulation or a slowdown? Breaking it down like that is more informative than the headline numbers, because it tells people what evidence would move you. It also makes it easier to update in public without looking like you're flip-flopping. If you said in advance "if this benchmark falls, or this much compute gets deployed, I'll shift earlier," then shifting is just your model working as intended.

And finally, some humility about the track record. Expert forecasts in this area have moved around a lot in recent years, mostly toward shorter timelines. That's not a reason to ignore forecasts, but it is a reason to hold them loosely and to communicate them as a current best estimate rather than a confident prophecy. What you want to avoid is both false precision and the opposite failure, where people say "nobody knows," and that gets heard as "so we needn't do anything." Deep uncertainty that includes substantial near-term probability is itself a strong reason to act.

r001.rationale: It recommends communicating a whole probability distribution over AGI arrival timing and giving dates for the 10%, 50%, and 90% probabilities.

r002.rationale: It recommends sharing several percentile dates, but does not identify an interval of possible arrival years as a lay-friendly format.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing is to be honest that this is a case where our uncertainty is really deep, and that it's a different kind of uncertainty from the sort you have about, say, whether it'll rain tomorrow. There's a tendency to reach for a single number — "2035," or "sometime in the next decade" — and that number ends up getting quoted and passed around as though it were the view, when really it was the median of a very wide distribution, and the person giving it may have had very little confidence in it.

So I'd much rather see people communicate the shape of their beliefs than a point estimate. Give a range. Say what you'd put at the tenth percentile and the ninetieth, and be willing to have those be quite far apart. If you genuinely think there's a real chance of transformative AI within five years and also a real chance it takes more than forty, say both of those things out loud, because that's the thing that actually matters for decision-making. The tails are where a lot of the action is.

The second thing is to be explicit about what the forecast is conditional on, and what you'd update on. A good forecaster can say, "Here's what I expect, and here's what would make me move my estimate earlier, and here's what would make me move it later." That's much more useful to a listener than a date, because it tells them what to watch for. It also makes the forecast falsifiable in a way that a vague "sometime soon" never is.

I'd also encourage people to separate out the different sources of uncertainty. Some of it is about the technology — how far current approaches scale, whether there are bottlenecks we haven't hit yet. Some of it is about definitions — what counts as AGI is itself contested, and two people can disagree about the date while actually agreeing about what the world will look like. And some of it is about the social and economic response. Disentangling those helps a lot, because otherwise disagreements that are really about definitions get mistaken for disagreements about the facts.

And finally, I think there's a humility point. We've been wrong about this before, in both directions. People in the 1960s thought it was a couple of decades away; people in the 2000s thought it was essentially off the table. Our track record of forecasting this particular thing isn't great, and I think that should show up in how we talk. Not as a reason to say nothing — I think refusing to give any estimate is its own kind of failure — but as a reason to hold our numbers loosely and to say so.

r001.rationale: Recommends communicating the shape of beliefs rather than a point estimate, including tenth- and ninetieth-percentile arrival years and a wide distribution.

r002.rationale: Explicitly recommends giving a range and illustrates it with possible arrival within five years or after forty years.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to communicate a distribution over dates, rather than just a single year. If someone says, “My best guess is 2040,” it’s very easy to hear that as, “We’ve got until 2040.” But they might actually assign a substantial probability to it arriving much sooner, and also a substantial probability to it taking much longer.

And those possibilities can matter more for decisions than the central estimate. If you’re considering a safety programme that will take ten years, you want to know the probability that AGI arrives before you finish, not just the forecaster’s median date.

I’d also want people to distinguish uncertainty within their forecast from uncertainty about the forecasting method itself. You can draw a very precise-looking curve, but that doesn’t mean we have strong grounds for its shape. So I’d give probabilities for a few time horizons, explain what I mean by AGI, and say something about the assumptions driving the forecast—and what evidence would change my mind.

r001.rationale: It explicitly recommends communicating “a distribution over dates” and giving probabilities for time horizons.

r002.rationale: It does not recommend an interval or range of possible arrival years as a lay-friendly format; it contrasts a single year with a distribution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most important thing is to give a distribution rather than just a date. If someone says, “I think AGI will arrive in 2040,” it’s very hard to know what they mean. Is that the point by which they think there’s a 50% chance? And do they think it’s almost certainly going to happen within five years of that, or could it be a century later?

Those are very different views, with very different implications. So I’d like people to say something like, “Here’s the probability I assign to it happening within ten years, within twenty years, and by the end of the century.” And to leave room for the possibility that it doesn’t happen at all.

I also think you need to distinguish uncertainty within your model from uncertainty about whether you’re using the right model. You might have a fairly precise extrapolation of recent progress, but be much less confident that the extrapolation will continue to apply. The precision of the calculation shouldn’t disguise that deeper uncertainty.

For decisions, the tails can matter enormously. You don’t have to think that AGI is likely in the next few years to think that the chance is substantial enough that we ought to prepare. Communicating that clearly is much more useful than giving people a single year to argue about.

r001.rationale: The response recommends giving a distribution and suggests assigning probabilities to AGI arriving within ten years, within twenty years, and by century’s end.

r002.rationale: It uses time intervals and bounds—such as within five years, within ten or twenty years, or much later—as concrete ways to make uncertainty easier to understand.
